summary.text: A woman in her early 40s was seen for routine assessment in an inflammatory bowel diseases clinic. She had ulcerative colitis pancolitis diagnosed in 1999 and large duct primary sclerosing cholangitis diagnosed in 2022, with no known history of endometriosis and no other past medical history.

Treatment history included steroids and 6-mercaptopurine before vedolizumab, which was commenced in early 2022 and dose-escalated in late 2022 for ongoing progressive disease activity and a rectal stricture on endoscopy. Current medications were vedolizumab four weekly, 6-mercaptopurine and mesalazine. She developed steroid dependency and complications of steroid-induced osteoporosis, and had an unknown reaction to azathioprine.

She reported occasional abdominal pain and bloating, daily bowel opening without diarrhoea or blood, infrequent menorrhagia and minor dysmenorrhoea; vital signs were normal with a benign abdominal examination. She denied smoking or alcohol and her family history was unremarkable for colorectal cancer.

Biochemical results were unremarkable, with haemoglobin 124 g/L, C-reactive protein 6.9 mg/L, albumin 36 g/L and faecal calprotectin 52 ug/g. Colonoscopy in 2022 demonstrated a rectosigmoid stricture; disease activity at time of colonoscopy (examination not identified) was scored by colon segment (UCEIS 3, 2 and 3-4); the stricture was recurrently biopsied and dilated over the next 18 months and repeated histology showed no dysplasia.

The differential diagnosis included malignant and benign strictures; malignancy was highly concerning given PSC and persistence of the stricture, while other benign causes were considered less likely. After a multidisciplinary meeting, definitive surgical management was recommended.

She underwent laparoscopic total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy in early 2024. Histology showed no active colonic inflammation and endometriosis of the rectal submucosa and muscularis propria with muscular hypertrophy corresponding to the stricture, with positive oestrogen receptor immunohistochemistry confirming the diagnosis; the stricture was benign and secondary to endometriosis.

At review in gastroenterology and colorectal clinics she was recovering well with resolution of gastrointestinal and gynaecological symptoms and improvements in abdominal pain, bloating and dysmenorrhoea.
Reproductive history recorded one child conceived naturally and a menstrual cycle of normal length.
